paragraphs: §1 — Introduction: corporealization

We have already recounted of them, at the beginning of the preceding bab, their statements on corporealization and likeness, and what they reported in the "Shiʿur Qomah" of [God's] measures and limits — from the toes of the feet to the head. They said, at the end of the matter, that every day Michael binds the phylacteries upon His [the Creator's] head, and that from the sole of His foot to the limit of His stature is two hundred thirty-six thousand parasangs — contrary to the saying of Scripture [Job 11:7]: "הַחֵקֶר אֱלוֹהַּ תִּמְצָא? אִם עַד תַּכְלִית שַׁדַּי תִּמְצָא?" and His saying [Isa 40:18]: "וְאֶל מִי תְּדַמְּיוּן אֵל וּמַה דְּמוּת תַּעַרְכוּ לוֹ."
§2 — The "Otiyyot de-Rabbi ʿAqiva"

They said in the "Otiyyot de-Rabbi ʿAqiva" that the Creator — exalted and exalted — said: "I took Enoch son of Jared, and raised the head of his stature above you among all the tall of stature, and made his throne greater than My throne, and his glory greater than My glory." In those same "letters" they also said that the Creator — exalted — bound His hands with the hands of the righteous when He calls them in the Garden of Eden, and will say to them: "I have come to you only to eat and drink with you."
§3 — The "Book of Ishmael" — Meṭaṭron

They said in the book ascribed to "Ishmael" — which is the "Book of Meṭaṭron" — that Meṭaṭron binds the phylacteries each morning upon the head of the Creator — far exalted is our God above this! — and that every day, when the time comes for reciting the [chapter of] the Unification in the morning, Meṭaṭron stands in awe, trembling, and dread, and binds the phylacteries upon the head of the Creator; and that the height of Meṭaṭron's stature is the height of the seven heavens and the seven seas, and the height of the heights of the [angels]. And the Creator — magnified and exalted — sits upon His throne, and he [Meṭaṭron] stands on his feet and cannot bind the phylacteries until he stretches and raises his leg.
§4 — God prays, in the Talmud

They have mentioned in the Talmud that the Creator — exalted — prays; and they grounded this on His saying [Isa 56:7]: "וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי" — and that His prayer is that He says [B. Berakhot 7a]: "יְהִי רָצוֹן מִלְּפָנַי שֶׁיִּכְבְּשׁוּ רַחֲמַי אֶת כַּעֲסִי… וְאֶתְנַהֵג עִם בָּנַי בְּמִדַּת רַחֲמִים." Blessed is He to whom belong [all] prayers and praises; far exalted and far raised is our God and Creator above what the extreme defilers ascribe to Him.
§5 — No reward for studying Scripture without the rabbinic circle

They said in the "Chapters of the Fathers" that you have no reward for reading and studying Scripture except in the company of the Rabbanites, and followed this by saying [B. Bava Metsiʿa 33a]: "אֵלּוּ שֶׁעוֹסְקִין בַּמִּקְרָא — מִדָּה וְאֵינָהּ מִדָּה. בַּמִּשְׁנָה — מִדָּה וְנוֹטְלִין עָלֶיהָ שָׂכָר. בַּגְּמָרָא — אֵין לְךָ מִדָּה גְּדוֹלָה מִזּוֹ. וּלְעוֹלָם הֱוֵי רָץ לַמִּשְׁנָה יוֹתֵר מִן הַמִּקְרָא." This contradicts the saying of Scripture [Josh 1:8]: "וְהָגִיתָ בּוֹ יוֹמָם וָלָיְלָה."
§6 — God weeps over the destruction

Scripture reported that, at the time of the Temple's destruction, mourning, weeping, and the like are obligatory on account of the transgressions, in His saying [Isa 22:11]: "וְלֹא הִבַּטְתֶּם אֶל יֹצְרָהּ" — closing [22:12]: "וַיִּקְרָא ה' צְבָאוֹת בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא לִבְכִי וּלְמִסְפֵּד." Yet they claimed, in "Tractate Ḥagigah" and in the "Answer of Ahab," that the weeping, the mourning, the sackcloth, and the ashes the Creator performed Himself. Does one who describes Him with weeping, mourning, and the wearing of sackcloth truly know God?
§7 — A hidden place

They said in the Talmud that God has a place called "the hidden places," in which He wept, per His saying [Jer 13:17]: "בְּמִסְתָּרִים תִּבְכֶּה נַפְשִׁי," and they said there that He says: "Woe to Me, that My house is destroyed and My children are exiled." They claimed that the angels surround Him, and that since His house was destroyed His stature is bent; and they said that He tears His hair with His hands, and that until now His judgment is not sealed. All this is contrary to the saying of Scripture [Job 26:14]: "וּמַה שֵּׁמֶץ דָּבָר נִשְׁמַע בּוֹ."
§8 — God learns from Moses

They said in the Talmud that when the Children of Israel grew slack in the Torah, the Creator became poor; they mean by it the Creator — exalted — by way of metaphor, lest a man ascribe the illness to His son. They grounded this on His saying [Eccl 10:18]: "בַּעֲצַלְתַּיִם יִמַּךְ הַמְּקָרֶה" — saying: the "roofing" (ha-meqareh) means only God, per [Ps 104:3]: "הַמְקָרֶה בַמַּיִם עֲלִיּוֹתָיו."
§9 — Aggadah: God learned three things from Moses

They said in their "Aggadah" known in the "Talmud of the school of Rabbi" that the Creator — exalted — learned from Moses three things. The first: from the story of the calf; when He wished to destroy the Children of Israel, saying [Exod 32:10]: "וְעַתָּה הַנִּיחָה לִּי וְיִחַר אַפִּי בָהֶם וַאֲכַלֵּם," Moses said to Him [Num 14:13]: "וְשָׁמְעוּ מִצְרַיִם כִּי הֶעֱלִיתָ בְכֹחֲךָ אֶת הָעָם הַזֶּה מִקִּרְבּוֹ," and [14:16]: "מִבִּלְתִּי יְכֹלֶת ה'" — and the Creator took notice [and refrained]. He said to the Creator: "You have given me life by Your word!"; and grounded it on His saying [Num 14:18]: "ה' אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב חֶסֶד." The second: that the Creator told Moses, in the story of Sihon, "וְהִתְגָּר בּוֹ מִלְחָמָה" [Deut 2:24] — yet Moses set this aside and did the opposite, in his saying [Deut 2:26]: "וָאֶשְׁלַח מַלְאָכִים מִמִּדְבַּר קְדֵמוֹת אֶל סִיחוֹן" with words of peace; and what he did was, with the Creator, the right thing. He said to him: "O Moses, I will annul My word and confirm yours!" — and accepted it from him, and used it thereafter, in His saying [Deut 20:10]: "כִּי תִקְרַב אֶל עִיר לְהִלָּחֵם עָלֶיהָ וְקָרָאתָ אֵלֶיהָ לְשָׁלוֹם." How far is anything more [a mark] of ignorance and feebleness than this, which they have ascribed to the [supposedly] All-Wise, of whom it is said [Dan 2:21]: "יָהֵב חָכְמְתָא לְחַכִּימִין וּמַנְדְּעָא לְיָדְעֵי בִינָה," who is the Giver of power to every possessor of power, of whom it is said [Ps 27 — i.e. the verse "from the LORD a man's steps…"], [Ps 147:5]: "גָּדוֹל אֲדוֹנֵינוּ וְרַב כֹּחַ," [147:10]: "לֹא בִגְבוּרַת הַסּוּס יֶחְפָּץ"?
§10 — One cannot go on enumerating

It would be beyond the power of the enumerator to count their statements of this kind; so we have confined ourselves to mentioning this small portion — by which their unbelief and irreligion are made clear, and the falsity of those who claim that they transmit from prophecy. Enough for you is what they reported in the Talmud concerning "Eliezer son of Hyrcanus": they said that a group of sages was disputing about which vessels become impure, until they reached the "Oven of Akhnai," made of separate pieces and rings, mounted one upon another, with a piece of clay between each two pieces and a gap between each piece — does this oven become impure or not? The rest of the sages judged it impure, and Eliezer did not. Every proof he brought, they did not accept from him. So he testified by signs. A first sign arose for him: the water that was flowing downward turned and flowed upward; they did not accept it. He testified by a second sign — that a carob tree uprooted itself and moved cubits from its place; they did not accept it. A third sign arose for him — that the walls of the study-house leaned; they did not accept it. When he saw this, he testified by a "bat qol" that came forth from heaven — and the meaning of this with them is the voice of the Creator — which said: "What have you with Eliezer, when the truth is with him?" And Joshua son of Hananiah arose and gestured toward heaven…
§11 — Song of Songs 7

He said [Song 7:6]: "מֶלֶךְ אָסוּר בָּרְהָטִים." And Eliezer already declared this in a "hymn" they pray on the Day of Atonement, "לְךָ הָאָרֶץ וְשׁוֹכְנֶיהָ," saying: "יַד ה' מְכֻוָּלָה." Perhaps this is what he [Muḥammad] said [Qurʾān 5, sūrat al-Māʾida 64]: "wa-qālat al-yahūd yad allāh maghlūla" — this fell to him and he took his saying from it.
§12 — Permitting fornication in black garments

What is more astonishing than their saying in the Talmud [B. Ḥagigah 16a]: "אִם רוֹאֶה אָדָם שֶׁיִּצְרוֹ מִתְגַּבֵּר עָלָיו, יֵלֵךְ לְמָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין מַכִּירִין אוֹתוֹ, וְיִלְבַּשׁ שְׁחוֹרִים וְיִתְעַטֵּף שְׁחוֹרִים, וְיַעֲשֶׂה מַה שֶּׁלִּבּוֹ חָפֵץ, וְאַל יְחַלֵּל שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא." By this saying they permitted lewdness and licentiousness — if a man wore black garments and went off to a place where he is unknown.
§13 — Meṭaṭron teaches in the Talmud; the story of Rabbah bar Naḥmani

They said in the Talmud that Meṭaṭron is a lesser god, whose name is "Kem Anadu," and that before him is an altar, and the souls of the righteous offer upon it, and the souls of the masters of the Talmud sit around him, and the angels stand erect before him, and he studies Talmud and halakha with them. They did not cease studying until they dissented over the words of Scripture [Lev 13:4]: "וְאִם בַּהֶרֶת לְבָנָה הִיא" — they said: it is pure; and the Creator said: it is impure. Those souls around him did not accept it from Him. He sent an angel to take the soul of "Rabbah son of Naḥmani," for this Rabbah was a learned man, an expert; and the angel could not take his spirit, for he heard him studying Talmud. He returned to the One who sent him and told Him the tale. The Sender said to him: "Stand over him like the knife, and set upon him a storm-wind; when he is silent, take his spirit." He did so, and his soul went up saying: "Pure, pure!" — praises to the Creator, exalted — siding with His judgment. The Creator — exalted — said: "They have defeated Me!"

This resembles the story we told of Eliezer son of Hyrcanus, and the Creator's saying: "My children have defeated Me!" In it is of [the same] good and abundance as in this and more. They said: out of honor for the soul of this "son of Naḥmani," his body was not given to the dogs. A scrap of a scroll was cast down from heaven to the academy of the people of Sura, written in it: that "Rabbah son of Naḥmani" had been summoned to guide the people of the Upper Academy. They arose and walked among the "marshes," the wildernesses, and the waters until they saw the birds and the vermin upon his corpse, and bore it and passed with it, and mourned three days. When they wished to part, another scrap fell from the cloud, written in it: "Whoever parts shall be among those put to death." So they returned to the gathering for seven days. Then a third scrap fell, [written in it]: "Return in peace." They left it and went. A storm-wind arose to destroy the world, for it wished to raise him up to heaven. One who asked — a man of the Arabs — said: "What is this?" They said to him: "'Son of Naḥmani' has been raised to heaven." Then he disputed with the Creator and said to Him: "You created 'son of Naḥmani,' and You took his spirit. Why ever do You destroy?" Then the wind was stilled.

At the beginning of this story — a story that Rabbah son of Naḥmani gave the Creator the lie, annulled His statement, and the Creator confessed His being defeated by him, and that "son of Naḥmani's" statement is the truth and His statement — that is, the Creator's — is the contrary. And at the end of the story — that the Arab gave the Creator pause, alerted Him that He wished to do what is not right, and that the Creator turned back from what He wished to do.
§14 — Mourning for Methuselah
They said that the Creator mourned for Methuselah seven days, per [Gen 7:10]: "וַיְהִי לְשִׁבְעַת הַיָּמִים וּמֵי הַמַּבּוּל."
§15 — God as a priest

They said that a man asked "Rav Abbahu," saying to him: "Is your God a priest?! — for He said [Exod 25:2]: 'וְיִקְחוּ לִי תְּרוּמָה.' If so, how, when He buried Moses — did He wash or immerse? If you say He washed in water — did He not say [Isa 40:12]: 'מִי מָדַד בְּשָׁעֳלוֹ מַיִם'? — for the water cannot contain Him or immerse Him." Rav Abbahu said: "He immersed in fire," and grounded it on His saying [Isa 66:15]: "כִּי הִנֵּה ה' בָּאֵשׁ יָבוֹא." He said: "And this is from the Torah, per His saying [Num 31:23]: 'כָּל דָּבָר אֲשֶׁר יָבֹא בָאֵשׁ תַּעֲבִירוּ בָאֵשׁ וְטָהֵר.'"
§16 — The Christians, and the claim about the "changes of the Seventy"

Thereafter they outdid the Christians in the very [matter of] contention and obstinacy; for the principles of the Christians in most of their statements rest on contention and obstinacy, since they used to acknowledge and recognize the truth of the legislation of the Jewish religion, and [then] abandoned it.

When it was made clear to them, in what was translated for them of our books, that alteration and exchange had already befallen it — they took up the effrontery to claim that the Greek language is the ancient tongue; this is reported of "Kūfarī" and his like. Many of them claim that no alteration or exchange befell the translation — saying that Ptolemy the king gathered seventy elders of the Jews, separated them, set each two of them in [their own] place, and commanded them to translate the twenty-four books. They did so. The translations were collated — no difference was found among them. This is what they call "the Production of the Seventy." As for the Rabbanites, they affirm this statement of theirs, and call the king who did this "Talmiyos" (Ptolemy).

Only they claim that the Creator — exalted and exalted — taught them all to write one [and the same] thing; and that they [the Seventy] altered ten things from what is in Scripture, writing them contrary to what they are. These are the things they claim the Seventy altered:

[Gen 1:1] "בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים בְּרֵאשִׁית" (for "בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים"); [1:26] "אֶעֱשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצֶלֶם וּדְמוּת" (for "נַעֲשֶׂה"); [1:27] "זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בְּרָאוֹ" (for "בְּרָאָם"); [2:2] "וַיְכַל אֱלֹהִים בַּיּוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי וַיִּשְׁבֹּת בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי" (for "הַשְּׁבִיעִי"); [Gen 49:6] "וּבִרְצֹנָם עִקְּרוּ אֵבוּס" (for "שׁוֹר"); [Exod 4:20] "וַיִּקַּח מֹשֶׁה אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ וְאֶת בָּנָיו וַיַּרְכִּבֵם עַל נוֹשֵׂא אֲנָשִׁים" (for "הַחֲמֹר"); [Num 16:15] "חֹמֶד אֶחָד מֵהֶם" (for "חֲמוֹר"); [Lev 11:6 / Deut 14:7] "הָאַרְנֶבֶת קְצַרַת הָרַגְלַיִם" (for "אַרְנֶבֶת"); [Exod 12:40] "וּמוֹשַׁב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר יָשְׁבוּ בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם וּבְכָל הָאֲרָצוֹת" (for [Egypt] alone); [Deut 4:19] "אֲשֶׁר חָלַק ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֹתָם לְהָאִיר לְכָל הָעַמִּים" (for "לְכֹל הָעַמִּים").

By this saying they ascribed to the Creator — exalted — distortion and the teaching of falsehood; and this is the utmost of corruption, for one who teaches falsehood and dictates it has [thereby] done falsehood, and one who did falsehood has lied. This is one of the things charged against the "Ḥabariyya" (the extremists).

[And the rejoinder: if the Creator altered the direction of these things, gathered by the Seventy, because they affect anthropomorphism — then He would have been obliged to alter the other verses too in which there are limbs: hand, eye, ear, mouth, and indeed the first verse of Genesis "אֲשֶׁר בָּרָא"; and ought He not to have altered [Exod 33:11]: "פָּנִים אֶל פָּנִים" which suggests speaking face to face? And so on; what is in Scripture of this kind the enumerator could not count. So their falsehood is exposed: for those very things they claimed were altered and exchanged are found among the Christians exactly as they are found with us, without alteration. The proof of this is that the Christians argue against us, to establish their statement of corporealization, by the saying of Scripture (Gen 1:26): "בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ."]

And the opening of the Torah with them [the Aramaic Targum of Gen 1:1] is "בְּקַדְמִין בְּרָא אֱלָהָא." With this — there is enough in recounting all that has been said of them. Is there [need] to end with this very [matter]?
§17 — The admission of "scandal"

This is what has been exposed of [my] taking from their statements. Among them is one who, if any of this is mentioned before him, says: "This is a scandal!" Among them are those who claim that not all the Rabbanites say this, but only the rare one among them. It has even reached me that some of them say these things are not the Rabbanites' statement, but that the dissenters composed them and slipped them into the statements of the Rabbanites.

So know this: if they take you up this way and pour [this] upon you, make use of curses against whoever said this and whoever knows that the Rabbanites said it and yet denies and multiplies [denials] — that you may suppress them by it. It had been my wish to argue in several things I have recounted of their statements — of what does not enter into the discussion of the commandments, such as their statement on corporealization, and that this Torah is not the Torah that Moses brought, and the like — and to refute what they claim of [received] tradition and transmission; but I have deferred this until I finish recounting what each sect held as distinctive, so that the response to them and to others may come one after another.
§18 — The "Targum of Onqelos"

They have magnified the matter of the "Targum of Onqelos" of the Torah, and magnified it greatly, to the point that they claimed that Onqelos the proselyte uttered it from his mouth ("jāʾi, wa-rūyā, wa-malāʾi"), and joined it to the Torah of God, reading it with [the Torah] verse by verse. In it are wonders beyond measure; of this — his saying at [Gen 49:11] "אֹסְרִי לַגֶּפֶן עִירֹה," which he rendered "in his town" (his city); and the rendering of [Deut 23:18] "לֹא תִהְיֶה קְדֵשָׁה" — that he meant a daughter of Israel should not be married to a [male] slave, nor a son of Israel to a bondwoman; and he rendered [Exod 12:48] "וְכָל עָרֵל לֹא יֹאכַל בּוֹ" — that every apostate from Judaism shall not eat of it; and he rendered [Gen 28:21] "וְהָיָה ה' לִי לֵאלֹהִים" — "and the word of the LORD shall be God to me."

With this — he dissented from the Rabbanites in several things. Of this — his saying that Enoch died, while they generally say he ascended to heaven alive; and his saying that the yemamah is "shafninim," while they know it is a rooster.

: Otiyyot de-Rabbi ʿAqiva, an early esoteric midrash on the letters of the alphabet (so Nemoy; cf. Kaufmann Kohler, "Alphabet of Akiba ben Joseph," Jewish Encyclopedia I, 310–311).
: The ancient source thus warrants the figure of Enoch–Meṭaṭron as a "lesser god" — a theme Q returns to in §13.
: The "Book of Ishmael" / Sefer Meṭaṭron, one of the Hekhalot works.

: Arabic taʿālā ilāhunā ʿan dhālika ʿuluwwan kabīran ("far exalted is our God above this!") — a Muslim formula (cf. Qurʾān 17:43) here adopted by Q, witnessing the linguistic integration of his Baghdadi-Arabic world.
: I.e. the Shemaʿ, the principal declaration of God's Unity.
: B. Berakhot 7a. Q cites it as an inconsistency: if God prays, to whom does He pray?
: B. Bava Metsiʿa 33a — Scripture, Mishnah, Gemara. Q reads the rabbinic preference for Mishnah over Scripture as undermining the Torah's own authority.
: Tractate Ḥagigah (cf. 5b); the "Answer of Ahab" is not a known source — perhaps an aggadah otherwise unattested to Q.
: B. Berakhot 3a.
: An allusion to the rabbinic exegesis of Eccl 10:18 / the "impoverishment" theme; the precise locus is uncertain.
: Midrash on Exod 14 / Num 14 and parallels; the "Talmud of the school of Rabbi" is Q's designation.
: The aggadah of God "learning" from Moses, which Q presses as an absurdity contradicting the kalām principle of absolute divine knowledge.
: Cf. Midrash Deuteronomy Rabbah 2 and parallels.
: B. Bava Metsiʿa 59b, the famous "Oven of Akhnai." Q uses it as a case of rabbinic "defeat" of God's own ruling. Cf. bab 2, §6 and bab 3, §16.

: Qurʾān, sūrat al-Māʾida (5):64, "wa-qālat al-yahūd yad allāh maghlūla" ("the Jews said: God's hand is fettered"). Q suggests Muḥammad may have heard the liturgical phrase "yad ha-shem mekhuvvala" (from a piyyuṭ of Eliezer ha-Qallir) and drawn the Qurʾānic verse from it.
: B. Ḥagigah 16a, the well-known saying about one whose [evil] inclination overpowers him.
: B. Sanhedrin 38b / Ḥagigah 14b — the story of Meṭaṭron as a "lesser god."
: The name "Kem Anadu," a polysemous name with roots in Hekhalot mysticism; cf. Scholem on the names of Meṭaṭron.
: B. Bava Metsiʿa 86a, the death of Rabbah bar Naḥmani.
: Arabic ḥidād (mourning); Genesis Rabbah 32.
: B. Rosh ha-Shanah 17b and aggadic parallels.
: "Kūfarī" (Nemoy: "Kafrī"), an unidentified Christian philosopher; possibly an allusion to a Church Father.

: The "ten alterations of the Seventy," a Talmudic tradition (B. Megillah 9a) of the changes the Septuagint translators allegedly made; Q deploys it to show that it contradicts [their claim of] the divine fidelity of the text.

: Arabic al-mujbira / al-ḥabariyya, "the extremists"/"the zealous devotees" — a Muslim sect that held the Qurʾān eternal; Q applies the label to any who claim the eternity of a divine utterance, needling the Rabbanites as their like.
: Targum Onqelos to Gen 1:1.
: The Aramaic Targum of the Torah ascribed to Onqelos the proselyte.
: Arabic transliterating three Hebrew words ("come, and see, and full"); the exact reading is uncertain and may be corrupt.
: Arabic shafninīm (doves); Onqelos renders the yemamah otherwise than the Rabbanites' interpretation. (So Nemoy.)
